analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the capital gains tax on asset sales for two years.
analysis.headline: The bill to make capital gains tax-free for two years was introduced with 9 cosponsors, all Republicans, and died in the Ways and Means Committee without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code so that any profit from selling a capital asset—stocks, bonds, businesses, real estate held as an investment—would be excluded from taxable income for two years [S2][S3]. Today, long-term gains are taxed at rates up to 20%. Wiping out the tax entirely would mean the biggest winners are the households that own most of the appreciated assets; the federal government would forgo the revenue, which must be made up through borrowing or other taxes [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Investors selling appreciated assets—stocks, bonds, business interests, and investment real estate—would pay no federal tax on the profit. Asset ownership is heavily concentrated among the wealthiest households, so the benefits would flow disproportionately to them.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a provision to the tax code excluding gain from the sale or exchange of any capital asset from gross income, meaning the profit would be untaxed [S3].
The exclusion would apply to sales and exchanges after enactment and would terminate two years after the bill became law [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers overall, since the Treasury would collect no capital gains revenue during the two-year window. The lost revenue would either add to the deficit or need to be offset by other taxes or cuts; the bill includes no offsets [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no revenue offset, so the full cost of the two-year exclusion would be added to the deficit unless Congress separately raised taxes or cut spending [S3].

Because capital gains are concentrated among the highest-income households, the exclusion would primarily cut taxes for a narrow, wealthy group rather than for typical wage earners, whose income is taxed as ordinary wages regardless [S2][S3].

A temporary two-year exclusion creates an incentive to time asset sales into the window, shifting activity without necessarily producing the new investment or job growth the bill's title suggests; the record contains no evidence for the jobs claim [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit case rests on the idea that untaxed gains would unlock capital and create jobs, but the bill's own text contains no mechanism tying the tax cut to new investment or hiring—it excludes gains on any sale of any capital asset by any holder. The direct effect is to eliminate a tax that falls almost entirely on the top of the income distribution, with the revenue loss borne by the Treasury. As drafted, the cost falls on the general public while the gain is concentrated among asset owners.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chuck Fleischmann introduced the Growing Jobs Through Capital Act of 2011 on November 2, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
Nine House Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action beyond the initial referral [S5].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill expired without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers as a whole, since the two-year capital gains holiday never took effect and the concentrated tax benefit for asset holders never materialized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; the targeted tax cut died

sides.party_line_note: All 10 supporters on record (the sponsor plus 9 cosponsors) were Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so no one had to oppose it on the record; the Ways and Means Committee, which took no action, was chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated federal tax on their profits from selling stocks, businesses, and investment real estate for two years. Gains on such assets are concentrated among the wealthiest households, so the tax cut would go overwhelmingly to them while the revenue loss lands on the Treasury.

A two-year window with zero capital gains tax would create strong incentive to buy and sell assets before the deadline, generating trading fees and commissions. The revenue loss to fund the same government would fall elsewhere in the economy.
